list.listitem: Obtain objective proof, when possible, of the time, quantity, and amount of the ingested product. C
Treatment is supportive. C
Ipecac or cathartic treatment should not be used; activated charcoal may prevent further absorption of ingested phenobarbital if given within 60 minutes of ingestion. C
The primary toxicity of barbiturate overdose is respiratory depression, which can lead to death. A common cause is therapeutic intoxication in infants and children.

The mechanism of action of barbiturates appears to be stimulation at the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor. GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter present in the CNS. Barbiturates may also block a subtype of the glutamate receptor, which is an excitatory neurotransmitter.
The combined action on both these receptors results in CNS depression which, in turn, causes respiratory depression by blocking central respiratory drive.
Pentobarbital infusions may contain propylene glycol; at high doses, this may result in propylene glycol toxicity.
Obtain history and objective proof, if possible, of the ingested product and the time and quantity.
Determine whether other products were ingested.
Nystagmus, slurred speech, ataxia, and altered level of consciousness can occur with mild barbiturate intoxication.
Moderate barbiturate poisoning can result in hyporeflexia and respiratory depression.
More severe cases of barbiturate poisoning result in coma, hypotension, and apnea.

In children, barbiturate poisoning can present with additional signs and symptoms such as muscle twitching, lack of sucking, lethargy, fever, skin rash, hepatic inflammation, alopecia, myocardial failure, and syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone.,
Qualitative and quantitative tests of barbiturates can detect barbiturates in serum and urine, though they do not always correlate with clinical severity.
The therapeutic level of phenobarbital is 15 to 40 μg/ml (65-172 μmol/L).
A serum level greater than 50 μg/ml (215 μmol/L) may be associated with coma, especially in a patient who is not a chronic barbiturate user.
Levels greater than 80 μg/ml (344 μmol/L) are potentially fatal.
Testing for alcohol, salicylate, acetaminophen, and other possibly coingested drugs should be considered.
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation). Do not give ipecac or activated charcoal without recommendation from a poison center or emergency department.
Naloxone and flumazenil are not effective for reversal of symptoms.
Dialsysis has been reported to be effective in case reports when other measures have failed.
Ipecac has not been shown to improve patient outcomes.

Activated charcoal may increase elimination of phenobarbital, though it has not been shown to decrease morbidity or mortality. It should only be given to patients who can protect their airway or are intubated.
Activated charcoal plus whole bowel irrigation has been used successfully to avoid dialysis.
Ipecac should not be used unless a life-threatening amount of phenobarbital has been ingested and treatment can be started within 60 minutes.
Cathartics should not be used.
Follow-up for overdose should include a mental health evaluation for concerns for self-harm and other mental heath needs.

Death is uncommon with barbiturate overdose. However, due to barbiturates having a long half-life, an extended amount of time should be allowed before performing a brain death exam to ensure barbiturate clearance.
No long-term medical sequelae follow overdose.
